A bit of background on Consumer NZ.
We're a consumer research and advocacy organization.
We've been representing the interests of New Zealand consumers since
Let's cut to the chase. We've been calling for meaningful penalties under the
Fair Trading Act for many years.
We're really supportive of the fact that the bill increases penalties to the
greater of $5 million or three times the commercial gain or loss avoided,
or the value of the relevant transaction.
I'll kind of break that down on why we support each of those
in a second. We think this is a significant but necessary
shift.
The purpose of a penalty is not simply to
punish a business after the event.
It's to deter behavior and the harm from that behavior before it
occurs. Penalties need to be high enough that complying with
the law is always the rational commercial choice.
If the cost of non-compliance is lower than the benefit gained, then the law
becomes part of a business risk calculation,
and that's not good enough for consumers, and it's not fair to the many businesses
who do do the right thing.
For too long, penalties for breaches of the Fair Trading Act have been too low to
act as an effective deterrent, particularly for larger
businesses. We see the consequences of weak deterrents and the
kinds of Fair Trading Act breaches Consumer NZ has repeatedly raised
concerns about. Misleading or inaccurate prices, promotions that are
not genuine, hidden or unavoidable fees, greenwashing and
other misleading environmental claims, and dodgy claims about
products or services that are difficult for consumers to
test before they buy.
These are not abstract legal problems.
They affect household budgets and consumer trust every
day. The Fair Trading Act is one of the core pieces of legislation that
underpins confidence in markets.
It sets the baseline expectation that businesses must not mislead
consumers or engage in unfair conduct.
But a baseline only works
if the consequences for breaching are meaningful.
Repeated breaches in the grocery sector, for example, are ubiquitous,
and they're a great example of where the current law is failing to deter
misleading conduct in relation to inaccurate shelf pricing
or misleading discounting, and where the current maximums are not
enough to incentivize the duopoly to modernize these systems.
If they were,
cases wouldn't currently be before the courts under the Fair Trading Act.
Meaningful Fair Trading Act penalties can help mitigate some of the
harm caused by the lack of meaningful competition in that
and other sectors in the economy.
This matters even more in the current cost of living environment.
New Zealanders are watching every dollar.
If the shelf price is wrong, or if a special is not really a saving,
if green claims are false, or if unavoidable fees are revealed late in the
transaction, consumers are not just inconvenienced, they may pay
more than expected, lose confidence in the market, or be forced to
spend time and energy trying to resolve a problem they never should have faced.
Similarly, with better deterrence, the Commerce Commission would need to
spend less of its investigative and enforcement budget on
businesses who should know better and have the capacity to comply,
like the supermarkets or the airlines or the banks or the
telcos,
but see compliance as a cost of doing business.
International platform businesses like Meta or Google
likely question whether existing penalties are a joke when they compare
them to other jurisdictions.
A penalty regime that can take into account commercial gain is
therefore important, and we strongly support this aspect of the bill.
It helps ensure that businesses cannot profit from misconduct.
It also means penalties can better reflect the size and seriousness of the
conduct, rather than being capped at a level that may be significant for small
businesses but immaterial for a very large one.
We also support the move to a civil
liability regime.
That should make enforcement more efficient and allow the Commerce Commission to
respond more effectively.
It is appropriate that the most serious and deliberate misconduct remains criminal,
but for many breaches, a civil regime should provide a more practical and faster
route to accountability. Lowering the standard of proof to the balance of
probability should also assist in encouraging the Commerce Commission to take
more cases.
However, increased penalties will only be effective as a
deterrent if the commission is seen as a credible threat.
The commission must be appropriately resourced to investigate and bring
cases. The courts must have clear powers to
impose penalties that both reflect the harm caused
and the benefit obtained.
